subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Why does a large organism need specialised gas-exchange surfaces while a single-celled organism does not?
options: A large organism has a small surface area to volume ratio, so simple diffusion alone is too slow
Large organisms do not need oxygen
questions.explain: Large organisms have a small surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion over the body surface is too slow.

questions.q: By which process do oxygen and carbon dioxide move across the alveolar wall?
questions.explain: Gases move down their concentration gradients by diffusion across the thin alveolar walls.

questions.q: Why does anaerobic respiration release less energy than aerobic respiration per glucose molecule?
options: Glucose is only partially broken down
questions.explain: Without oxygen glucose is incompletely broken down, so less energy is released.

questions.q: What lines the trachea and bronchi to trap dust and microbes?
questions.explain: Sticky mucus traps particles and cilia sweep it away from the lungs.

questions.q: Which structure carries air from the throat towards the lungs?
questions.explain: The trachea (windpipe) carries air down towards the bronchi and lungs.

questions.q: Compared with inhaled air, exhaled air contains...
options: Less oxygen and more carbon dioxide
More oxygen and less carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Exhaled air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide because oxygen is used in respiration.

questions.q: In which organelle does most aerobic respiration occur?
questions.explain: Aerobic respiration takes place mainly in the mitochondria.

questions.q: How could you show that small organisms such as germinating seeds are respiring?
options: They release carbon dioxide and warmth
questions.explain: Respiring seeds release carbon dioxide and energy as heat, which can be detected experimentally.

questions.q: Where does gas exchange take place in the lungs?
questions.explain: The alveoli are tiny air sacs where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.

questions.q: Anaerobic respiration means respiration that takes place...
questions.explain: Anaerobic respiration is the release of energy from glucose without using oxygen.

questions.q: In a leaf, which structures allow gases to enter and leave?
questions.explain: Stomata are small pores, mainly on the lower leaf surface, that allow gas exchange.

questions.q: What happens to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles when we breathe in?
options: Diaphragm contracts and flattens, intercostal muscles contract
questions.explain: During inhalation the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the intercostal muscles raise the ribs, increasing chest volume.

questions.q: Which is an adaptation of alveoli for efficient gas exchange?
options: Large surface area, thin moist walls and good blood supply
questions.explain: Alveoli have a large surface area, thin moist walls and rich blood supply to maximise diffusion.

questions.q: Aerobic respiration releases more energy per glucose molecule than anaerobic respiration because...
options: glucose is completely broken down using oxygen
questions.explain: With oxygen, glucose is fully broken down, releasing much more energy than anaerobic respiration.

questions.q: Which gas diffuses from the alveoli into the blood?
questions.explain: Oxygen diffuses from the high concentration in the alveoli into the blood.

questions.q: Why is the air we breathe in warmed and moistened in the airways?
options: To protect the delicate alveoli and help gases dissolve
questions.explain: Warming and moistening the air protects the lungs and helps gases dissolve before diffusing.

questions.q: Which statement about respiration and breathing is correct?
options: Respiration only happens in the lungs
Respiration is a chemical reaction in cells; breathing is the movement of air in and out
questions.explain: Respiration is a chemical reaction releasing energy in cells; breathing is just ventilation of the lungs.

questions.q: On which surface of a leaf are stomata usually most numerous?
questions.explain: Stomata are usually concentrated on the lower surface, reducing water loss.

questions.q: Plant and yeast cells respiring anaerobically produce ethanol; this process is also called...
questions.explain: Anaerobic respiration in yeast and plants is known as fermentation.

questions.q: Why can a build-up of lactic acid cause muscle fatigue and cramp?
options: It is mildly acidic and affects how muscles work
questions.explain: Lactic acid lowers pH in the muscle, contributing to fatigue and cramp.

questions.q: How is lactic acid eventually removed from the body after exercise?
options: Converted to glucose in the stomach
Breathed out as a gas in the lungs
Transported in the blood to the liver and broken down using oxygen
questions.explain: Lactic acid is carried in the blood to the liver, where it is oxidised once oxygen is available.

questions.q: Which gas diffuses from the blood into the alveoli to be breathed out?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli to be exhaled.
